items.title: Nabad iyo Nolol oo caddeysay mowqifkeeda warqadii ay mucaaradka u direen caalamka
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – Wasiirkii hore ee Arrimaha Dibadda Soomaaliya, Maxamed Cabdirisaaq Maxamuud ayaa sheegay in xisbiga Nabad iyo Nolol uu si cad uga soo horjeedo soo jeedin kasta oo ku baaqeysa in Soomaaliya dib loogu celiyo nidaamka KMG ah. Warqadda uu Golaha Mustaqbalka si toos ah diray dalalka ay ciidamadoodu qeybta ka yihiin howl-galka AUSSOM iyo saaxiibada caalamiga ah ayaa loogu jeediyay in loo baahan yahay dhismaha gole KMG ah, si loo badbaadiyo sharciyadda iyo kalsoonida. Maxamed Cabdirisaaq ayaa sheegay in Nabad iyo Nolol oo uu hoggaamiyo Madaxweynihii hore ee Soomaaliya Maxamed Cabdullaahi Farmaajo, uusan marnaba taageersanayn in dalka dib loogu celiyo marxaladdii KMG ahayd, isagoo xusah in Soomaaliya ay soo dhaaftay heerkaas. “Ku noqoshada nidaamkii ku-meel-gaarka ahaa waxay noqon lahayd dib u dhac siyaasadeed, mana aha xal waara oo lagu wajahayo caqabadaha maanta jira,” ayuu yiri Maxamed Cabdirisaaq oo sheegay in loo baahan yahay in la ilaaliyo horumarka dowlad-dhiska ee dalka laga gaaray. Sidoo kale wuxuu Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud ku dhaliilay in dalka u horseeday heer mar kale lagu fikiro suurtagalnimada in dalka dib loogu celiyo marxaladdii ku-meel-gaarnimadii. Cabdirisaaq ayaa ku dooday in halkii dib loogu laaban lahaa nidaam KMG ah ay habboon tahay in dhinacyada siyaasadda Soomaaliya ay sii wadaan wada-hadallada iyo dadaallada lagu raadinayo is-afgarad, isagoo xusay in tanaasul, wadatashi iyo wada-xaajood ay yihiin waddada ugu habboon ee lagu xallin karo khilaafaadka taagan. Sidoo kale, wuxuu carrabka ku adkeeyay in xal kasta oo siyaasadeed uu ku saleysnaado heshiis ay wada gaaraan saamileyda siyaasadda dalka, si loo ilaaliyo xasilloonida iyo geeddi-socodka dowlad-dhiska, loogana fogaado tallaabooyin dib u dhac ku keeni kara hay’adaha dowladda. Hadalka wasiirkii hore ee arrimaha dibadda ayaa kusoo beegmaya xilli ay sii xoogeysanayaan doodaha siyaasadeed ee ku saabsan hannaanka doorashooyinka, dib-u-eegista dastuurka iyo awood-qaybsiga dalka, iyadoo dowladda iyo mucaaradka ay weli isku hayaan sida looga gudbi karo ismari-waaga siyaasadeed. Si kastaba, warqaddii Golaha Mustaqbalka Soomaaliyeed ayaa dhalisay falcelinno kala duwan oo ka imanaya dhinacyada siyaasadda, iyadoo qaar ay u arkaan waddo lagu gaari karo xal siyaasadeed, halka kuwo kalena, sida xisbiga Nabad iyo Nolol ay ku doodayaan in dib loogu laabto nidaamka KMG ah uu dhaawici karo horumarka ay Soomaaliya ka sameysay dib-u-dhiska dowladnimada. The post Nabad iyo Nolol oo caddeysay mowqifkeeda warqadii ay mucaaradka u direen caalamka appeared first on Caasimada Online .

items.title: China Offered Somaliland More Than a Quarter of a Billion Dollars to Drop Taiwan. Somaliland Said No.
items.description: China Offered Somaliland More Than a Quarter of a Billion Dollars to Drop Taiwan. Somaliland Said No. Getting to Somaliland used to be simple. Then Somaliland refused more than a quarter of a billion dollars to drop Taiwan, and the routes began closing. Mogadishu extended an air defense identification zone over the whole territory, then built a visa system that barred Taiwanese passports, then Israeli ones, then anyone not born in Somalia. No warship was involved. Americans, Israelis and Taiwanese now fly into a small Ethiopian town of about 200,000 and drive ninety minutes to the land border. The method is the point: airspace and paperwork achieve what a blockade would, and the same tools work anywhere a country depends on one airport.   President Kagame and President Xi Jinping of China Joint Press Conference | Kigali, 23 July 2018 HARGEISA, SOMALILAND— Getting to Somaliland was once easy for diplomats, businessmen, and tourists alike. It was an easy connection via Ethiopian Airlines or from Fly Dubai, Emirates Airline’s low-cost partner. That changed just over a year ago. China’s Xi Jinping. Image Credit: Creative Commons. While the White House celebrated Taiwan’s July 2020 decision to recognize Somaliland, tweeting , “Great to see Taiwan stepping up its engagement in East Africa in a time of such tremendous need. Taiwan is a great partner in health, education, technical assistance, and more!” China was furious. Decades of U.S. diplomatic neglect allowed China to consolidate control over Africa. Beyond Somaliland, only the small, landlocked country Eswatini maintains relations with Taiwan . The Chinese embassy in Mogadishu sought an urgent meeting with Somaliland authorities and, according to both Somalilander and Taiwanese officials, promised more than a quarter billion dollars in assistance, but Somaliland held firm. While the country is impoverished, it is also principled. Both its clan structure and vibrant democratic culture make bribery in Chinese leadership more difficult, since secrecy is harder to maintain. Shame matters. Exposure of any leader taking bribes would be swift, and such exposure would stigmatize tens of thousands through clan association. This is why Chinese outreach toward Somaliland’s new president also failed. Bordering both Djibouti and Ethiopia, Somaliland officials also view the two countries as cautionary tales of the dangers of China’s debt-trap diplomacy. Unable to pry Somaliland away from Taiwan with carrots, China turned toward sticks. It instigated an insurgency in a far-flung Somaliland province. Beginning in April 2025, China encouraged the Somali government to overturn a 35-year status quo and challenge Somaliland’s airspace . Without State Department pushback, Mogadishu extended its Air Defense Identification Zone over all of Somaliland, requiring all aircraft to identify themselves for national security. Beijing demanded, via Mogadishu, denial of overflight and landing rights to aircraft carrying Taiwanese businessmen and development specialists. The Somali government also instituted an e-visa scheme, requiring anyone entering Somalia or Somaliland to first obtain a Mogadishu-issued e-visa, and subsequent ly outlawed Taiwanese and Israeli passports. By October 2025, as Americans, Brits, and Israelis began visiting and investing in Somaliland, China pressured Mogadishu to ban e-visas for all “Non-Somalia-born foreigners.” Hackers meanwhile accessed Somalia’s e-visa system and stole the data on 35,000 applicants, including their names, addresses, financial information, and photos, posing an immediate risk to both American servicemen and investors, especially given Mogadishu’s ties to China and Al-Shabaab’s infiltration of the Somali security forces. There are also military implications. With U.S. Africa Command increasingly interested in the Berbera airfield, the State Department’s acceptance of China and Somalia’s expanded Air Defense Identification Zone could undercut American efforts to counter the Houthis or run counter-terror operations in the Horn of Africa. For Somaliland, there are workarounds: Americans, Israelis, and Taiwanese can fly to Jigjiga, a small town of about 200,000, and then drive the 90-minute-or-so drive to Somaliland’s land border, though concerted pressure on Ethiopia could also endanger this route. The problem is that what happens in Somaliland does not stay in Somaliland . While the United States and Europe focus on threats to freedom of navigation at sea, China’s relative success in strangling pro-Western Somaliland provides a playbook for elsewhere. Wedged between South Africa and Mozambique, Eswatini depends entirely on one airport . Given its neighbors’ pro-China orientation and the State Department’s unwillingness to stand up for Taiwan, Israel, and even Americans in Somaliland, strangling Eswatini is a real threat. Perhaps the White House, State Department, and Pentagon do not care about such a small African kingdom, but the danger also extends to Latin America. Paraguay’s importance only grows, given its location and critical mineral wealth . Like Somaliland, Paraguay unapologetically embraces Taiwan and Israel. Absent any pushback on China’s weaponization of airspace, Beijing could seek to deny flights carrying Americans or Taiwanese into Paraguay’s main Silvio Pettirossi International Airport. China has become both a master of hijacking and weaponizing international systems and bureaucratic salami slicing : It encroaches on freedoms and operations, pauses to see if there is reaction from the United States and Europe, and then tightens the noose if not. Today, Somaliland and its airspace are the canary in the coal mine. If President Donald Trump truly wants to stand up for American businessmen and counter China’s efforts to dominate rare earths, he and Secretary of State Marco Rubio must act to instruct regional states to cease recognizing the Chinese desire for expanded control over airspace in the Horn of Africa before China can take its air denial model farther. About the Author: Dr. Michael Rubin Michael Rubin is director of policy analysis at the Middle East Forum and a distinguished fellow at India’s Usanas Foundation. A former Pentagon official, Dr. Rubin was a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute for more than two decades. He has lived in post-revolution Iran, Yemen, and both pre- and postwar Iraq. Opinions expressed here are the author’s own. In this article: Africa , China , featured , Israel Iran , Somalia , Somaliland , Taiwan , UK , World News Written By Michael Rubin Michael Rubin is a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and director of policy analysis at the Middle East Forum. A former Pentagon official, Dr. Rubin has lived in post-revolution Iran, Yemen, and both pre- and postwar Iraq. He also spent time with the Taliban before 9/11. For more than a decade, he taught classes at sea about the Horn of Africa and Middle East conflicts, culture, and terrorism, to deployed US Navy and Marine units. Dr. Rubin is the author, coauthor, and coeditor of several books exploring diplomacy, Iranian history, Arab culture, Kurdish studies, and Shi’ite politics.

items.title: U.S. Treasury Clarifies OFAC Sanctions Records; Hassan Dahir Aweys Remains Under U.S. and U.N. Sanctions
items.description: Washington (WDN) – The U.S. Department of the Treasury has carried out a broad administrative update of its sanctions database, prompting confusion in some quarters over whether veteran Somali Islamist figure Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys had been removed from the U.S. sanctions list. Official records make clear that he has not. The update, implemented by the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), is part of a wider effort to improve the accuracy, consistency, and usability of its sanctions database by eliminating duplicate entries, correcting outdated information, and consolidating multiple aliases into single records. Among those affected by the technical update was Hassan Dahir Aweys. However, the revision does not represent the lifting of U.S. sanctions against him. Administrative Update—Not Sanctions Relief The updated OFAC record continues to list Hassan Dahir Aweys as a sanctioned individual under the Somalia sanctions program. His file now consolidates numerous aliases previously scattered across multiple entries, including: Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys Hassan Dahir Awes Shaykh Hassan Dahir Awes and several additional spelling variations used over the years. The consolidation is intended to make sanctions screening more accurate for banks, financial institutions, and compliance officers, ensuring that all known aliases are linked to a single sanctioned individual rather than appearing as multiple independent records. OFAC’s sanctions database contains thousands of individuals, companies, and organizations worldwide. Over time, records can become increasingly complex because: sanctioned individuals often use multiple names or spellings; aliases accumulate over many years; organizations dissolve or change names; duplicate entries emerge; and outdated information requires correction. To improve efficiency and reduce compliance errors, OFAC periodically cleans and consolidates its records. Such updates are administrative in nature and should not be interpreted as the removal of sanctions unless OFAC explicitly announces a delisting. Hassan Dahir Aweys Remains Sanctioned Despite the restructuring of his record, Hassan Dahir Aweys remains fully designated under the U.S. Somalia sanctions program. He was originally added to OFAC’s sanctions list on April 13, 2010, pursuant to Executive Order 13536, which targets individuals accused of contributing to conflict and instability in Somalia. That designation remains in force. Consequently, any reports suggesting that the United States has removed Hassan Dahir Aweys from its sanctions list are inaccurate. What changed was the structure of his record—not his legal status. Individuals listed by OFAC remain subject to significant financial restrictions. Assets and property interests under U.S. jurisdiction may be frozen, while U.S. citizens, businesses, and institutions are generally prohibited from conducting transactions with designated individuals, depending on the applicable sanctions regime. The practical impact extends well beyond the United States. Banks and multinational financial institutions around the world routinely screen transactions against OFAC databases. A sanctioned individual appearing on those lists can face restrictions in international banking, financial transfers, and commercial dealings. Hassan Dahir Aweys also remains subject to United Nations sanctions. The U.N. Security Council designated him on April 12, 2010, under the Somalia sanctions regime established pursuant to Resolution 1844 (2008). The United Nations identified him as a senior political and ideological leader of armed Islamist groups operating in Somalia and concluded that his activities posed a threat to Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government and African Union peacekeeping forces. Like OFAC, the United Nations maintains multiple aliases for Aweys to ensure sanctions enforcement accurately identifies the individual regardless of the name variation used. Compliance experts note that administrative updates frequently generate misunderstanding because the removal or consolidation of a database entry can appear, at first glance, to resemble a sanctions delisting. In reality, the two are fundamentally different. For example, if one sanctioned individual has five separate aliases listed as independent records, financial institutions may mistakenly interpret them as five different people. Consolidating those aliases into a single master record improves accuracy without altering the individual’s legal status. That is precisely what occurred in the case of Hassan Dahir Aweys. No Change in Legal Status The latest OFAC update is therefore best understood as a technical modernization of the sanctions database rather than a policy decision. Hassan Dahir Aweys remains listed under both U.S. Treasury and United Nations sanctions. The administrative revision merely streamlines how his information appears in official databases, making sanctions screening more reliable for financial institutions worldwide. For banks, compliance officers, and government agencies, the message is clear: the record has been cleaned up—but the sanctions remain fully in force. items.fullContent: Washington (WDN) – The U.S. Department of the Treasury has carried out a broad administrative update of its sanctions database, prompting confusion in some quarters over whether veteran Somali Islamist figure Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys had been removed from the U.S. sanctions list. Official records make clear that he has not. The update, implemented by the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), is part of a wider effort to improve the accuracy, consistency, and usability of its sanctions database by eliminating duplicate entries, correcting outdated information, and consolidating multiple aliases into single records. Among those affected by the technical update was Hassan Dahir Aweys. However, the revision does not represent the lifting of U.S. sanctions against him. Administrative Update—Not Sanctions Relief The updated OFAC record continues to list Hassan Dahir Aweys as a sanctioned individual under the Somalia sanctions program. His file now consolidates numerous aliases previously scattered across multiple entries, including: Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys Hassan Dahir Awes Shaykh Hassan Dahir Awes and several additional spelling variations used over the years. The consolidation is intended to make sanctions screening more accurate for banks, financial institutions, and compliance officers, ensuring that all known aliases are linked to a single sanctioned individual rather than appearing as multiple independent records. OFAC’s sanctions database contains thousands of individuals, companies, and organizations worldwide. Over time, records can become increasingly complex because: sanctioned individuals often use multiple names or spellings; aliases accumulate over many years; organizations dissolve or change names; duplicate entries emerge; and outdated information requires correction. To improve efficiency and reduce compliance errors, OFAC periodically cleans and consolidates its records. Such updates are administrative in nature and should not be interpreted as the removal of sanctions unless OFAC explicitly announces a delisting. Hassan Dahir Aweys Remains Sanctioned Despite the restructuring of his record, Hassan Dahir Aweys remains fully designated under the U.S. Somalia sanctions program. He was originally added to OFAC’s sanctions list on April 13, 2010, pursuant to Executive Order 13536, which targets individuals accused of contributing to conflict and instability in Somalia. That designation remains in force. Consequently, any reports suggesting that the United States has removed Hassan Dahir Aweys from its sanctions list are inaccurate. What changed was the structure of his record—not his legal status. Individuals listed by OFAC remain subject to significant financial restrictions. Assets and property interests under U.S. jurisdiction may be frozen, while U.S. citizens, businesses, and institutions are generally prohibited from conducting transactions with designated individuals, depending on the applicable sanctions regime. The practical impact extends well beyond the United States. Banks and multinational financial institutions around the world routinely screen transactions against OFAC databases. A sanctioned individual appearing on those lists can face restrictions in international banking, financial transfers, and commercial dealings. Hassan Dahir Aweys also remains subject to United Nations sanctions. The U.N. Security Council designated him on April 12, 2010, under the Somalia sanctions regime established pursuant to Resolution 1844 (2008). The United Nations identified him as a senior political and ideological leader of armed Islamist groups operating in Somalia and concluded that his activities posed a threat to Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government and African Union peacekeeping forces. Like OFAC, the United Nations maintains multiple aliases for Aweys to ensure sanctions enforcement accurately identifies the individual regardless of the name variation used. Compliance experts note that administrative updates frequently generate misunderstanding because the removal or consolidation of a database entry can appear, at first glance, to resemble a sanctions delisting. In reality, the two are fundamentally different. For example, if one sanctioned individual has five separate aliases listed as independent records, financial institutions may mistakenly interpret them as five different people. Consolidating those aliases into a single master record improves accuracy without altering the individual’s legal status. That is precisely what occurred in the case of Hassan Dahir Aweys. No Change in Legal Status The latest OFAC update is therefore best understood as a technical modernization of the sanctions database rather than a policy decision. Hassan Dahir Aweys remains listed under both U.S. Treasury and United Nations sanctions. The administrative revision merely streamlines how his information appears in official databases, making sanctions screening more reliable for financial institutions worldwide. For banks, compliance officers, and government agencies, the message is clear: the record has been cleaned up—but the sanctions remain fully in force. items.title: Digital Press Briefing from the Africa Logistics and Communications Symposium, with the U.S. Department of Commerce and U.S. Department of War
items.description: Mark Mitchell, Deputy Assistant Secretary for the Office of Middle East and Africa, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce Brigadier General Paul G. Filcek, Director of Logistics, U.S. Africa Command Africa Regional Media Hub MODERATOR: Good afternoon, and welcome, journalists from across Africa, to the U.S. Department of State’s Africa Regional Media Hub. My name is Phillip Assis, and I’m the director of the hub. We are privileged to be joined today by Deputy Assistant Secretary Mark Mitchell from the Office of Middle East and Africa at the International Trade Administration within the U.S. Department of Commerce and by Brigadier General Paul G. Filcek, Director of Logistics at U.S. Africa Command. Please note that an earlier announcement for this call went out with Brigadier General Filcek’s prior title; the correct title is Director of Logistics at U.S. Africa Command. Both of our guests are joining us from the Africa Logistics and Communications Symposium, which is currently taking place in Ethiopia. Today’s briefing is on the record, and you may quote our two guests by name and title. We will begin today’s briefing with opening remarks by Deputy Assistant Secretary Mark Mitchell, and then by Brigadier General Paul G. Filcek, and then we will turn to your questions. And we’ll try to get to as many of your questions as we can during the briefing. With that, I am pleased to turn the floor over to Deputy Assistant Secretary Mark Mitchell. MR MITCHELL: Thank you, and good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for having me here. My name is Mark Mitchell, and I serve as United States Deputy Assistant Secretary of Commerce overseeing the Middle East and Africa. I’m wrapping up four productive days in Addis Ababa where I joined the African Logistics and Communications Symposium, and held many valuable meetings with the Government of Ethiopia, with Ethiopian Airlines, and a number of private sector partners. It was a pleasure to reconnect with General Anderson and to continue the strengthening of our relationship between the Department of Commerce and AFRICOM. It is a priority of mine since my first day in joining the Department of Commerce. With delegates from more than 40 countries in attendance, the African Logistics and Communications Symposium offered a truly continent-wide platform – a rare chance to put U.S. companies in front of nearly the entire whole of Africa at once. I had the chance to talk about how security underpins economic development and to meet with and promote those U.S. companies helping to deliver that security. The Strategic Infrastructure Investment Working Group, launched earlier this year by Deputy Secretary of State Landau together with the African Union, reflects that commitment. And it’s an initiative the Department of Commerce is well positioned to support going forward. American companies, particularly in logistics and communications, offer some of the best technology and quality available anywhere. That technology helps African nations build the security and the stability that will let the projects under this working group succeed. Being here in Ethiopia, I had the chance to see firsthand the opportunities this country holds for U.S. investors and companies. The timing of this visit was fortunate, coming just after the public-private dialogue the American Chamber of Commerce co-hosted with the Ethiopian Investment Commission last week – another step in the right direction for strengthening the business environment for U.S. companies here. By all accounts, that dialogue was a strong event, building on the reforms the Government of Ethiopia continues to advance – reforms that will open genuine opportunities for U.S. companies and further U.S.-Ethiopia development. One personal highlight for me was my meeting with Ethiopian Airlines. My father actually flew for them many years ago. So making that connection carried special meaning. We were able to discuss the Bishoftu International Airport project, which is remarkable and very exciting as an undertaking for the company, and indeed the country. Across agencies, the U.S. Government is committed to exploring ways to support the realization of this transformative project. And the Department of Commerce has closely engaged in pushing to secure strong United States participation. To that end, the partnership between Boeing and Ethiopian Airlines remains a point of pride for the United States and Ethiopia. We’re excited about what that airport’s expansion portends for the airline’s growth, meaning more Boeing aircraft powered by GE Aerospace engines in fact connecting Africa to the world further. Finally, another highlight of my visit was Ethiopia’s Artificial Intelligence Institute, where I can see real opportunity for U.S.-Ethiopia collaboration. The Department of Commerce has been tasked by the President with leading the United States Government’s strategy to promote export of the American AI tech stack, and we look forward to building on our earlier conversations here, and in that regard to support Ethiopia’s ambitious agenda in this space. Altogether, my visit here has reaffirmed for me the range of concrete, growing business opportunities for U.S. companies in Ethiopia and across Africa. Events like the African Logistics and Communications Symposium are exactly the kind of platform we need to keep creating to turn these opportunities into consequential new partnerships, and the Department of Commerce is here and committed to working so closely with our colleagues at AFRICOM and other agencies across the United States Government on that mission. Thank you. MODERATOR: Great. Thank you, Deputy Assistant Secretary Mark Mitchell. Brigadier General Paul G. Filcek, is there anything that you would like to add before we turn to our questions? BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Yes, thank you. Greetings to all and thank you for this opportunity to highlight an amazing week on the African continent. Assistant Secretary Mitchell and I will give you two different perspectives (inaudible) role as co-host, alongside the Ethiopian ministry of defense, of the 2026 Africa Logistics and Communications Symposium. I want to express how genuinely grateful we are to the people of Ethiopia and especially the Ethiopian ministry of defense for their willingness to partner with us for this event. Ethiopia clearly prioritizes logistics and communications and the fundamental interdependence of the two. We are honored (inaudible) communications form the foundation of everything we do in military operations, but more than that, they underpin the foundations of our modern societies. That is why we have, for the first time, deliberately combined our logistics and communications endeavors into a single conference. No amount (inaudible) if we can’t move them to points of need, effectively sustain them, or communicate quickly and effectively, the technology and the systems have no value. To put it more concisely, logistics and communications are the decisive edge because they set the limits of our operational capabilities. We are proud to have made history with the magnitude of this symposium. The 40 partner nations and 27 private industry attendees are both all-time records for a USAFRICOM-co-hosted functional event. Across the African continent we face growing and converging threats on our mutual security, safety, and prosperity, including human trafficking and a dramatic rise in illegal narcotics trafficking – now more than six times what it was just two years ago. Meeting and defeating these grave threats require cooperation, coordination, effective and reliable communications, and the ability to rapidly move people, equipment, and supplies to points of need, often over great distances and challenging conditions. History reminds us of how difficult World War 2 vast quantities of lend-lease equipment and supplies were transported across the continent to support allies, overcoming some of the harshest terrain and longest distances on Earth. That effort succeeded only because of deliberate investment in logistics nodes, air and land routes, and exceptional communications. The same fundamental requirements remain today. We must become ever smarter with our limited resources. We need greater interoperability and increasing (inaudible) partnerships. This symposium brings together these 40 partner nations and 27 companies precisely to foster this important dialogue – not just in the sessions but in the conversations outside the rooms. It is important to note that a central theme of this event is the powerful intersection of security and commercial investment that is the AFRICOM strategic element enabled by investments, creates stability which attracts even greater investments and drives toward prosperity. When our partners succeed, we succeed. The story of Ethiopian Airlines is a powerful example. Almost eight decades ago, those pioneers who dreamed of something great did so while recognizing up front that success depended on much more than airplanes and pilots. Sustained success could only be assured with significant investments in maintenance, repair, overhaul, depot operations, workforce training and development, and a robust supply chain. That foresight is why Ethiopian Airlines remains the leading carrier on the continent today. We stand in the inflection point. The digital age of expanding satellite constellations, networked drones, globally enabled communications, and accelerating artificial intelligence is rapidly changing not just warfare but the foundational structures of society. Our job is to experiment, adapt, test, learn, and move quickly to bring logistics and communications technologies and sustainment programs that actually work in African conditions. Logistics and communications, industry partnerships, regional cooperation and interoperability – these are not the exciting aspects of defense and security, but they are the elements that ultimately determine success or failure, victory or defeat. Our intent for this African Logistics and Communications Symposium is to strengthen our partnerships, share challenges that can generate shared solutions, and cultivate investments into capabilities that will keep our nation secure and our people protected. Thank you, and I welcome your questions. MODERATOR: Great, thank you. Thank you, Brigadier General Paul G. Filcek. We’ll now begin the question-and-answer portion of today’s briefing, but please be aware that it will not be possible to answer all of your questions in the short time that we have today. With that, our first question today will go to Fishe Media from Nigeria, who asked about competing global influence. And his question is – this is directed to DAS Mitchell – “African nations are engaging with the United States, China, the European Union, Türkiye, and Gulf States all at once. What unique value does the United States believe it brings to African partners that sets it apart from these other players?” MR MITCHELL: Thank you for the question. It’s true, African nations today have more options for global partners than ever, and that is a good thing. Here’s the value proposition that I think sets the United States apart. First, the U.S. approach is rooted in long-term enterprise-driven partnership, not one-off transactions. Our private sector invests for the long term, helping to build durable commercial ecosystems that strengthen the local institutions, they’re deep in the regulatory capacity, and that expand opportunities for African firms and workers. We see this in sectors like energy, digital infrastructure, critical minerals, and logistics, all areas where American companies deliver world-class technology, transparency, and high-standard operations that reinforce resilience and good governance. Second, the United States brings high-quality finance, trusted standards, and risk mitigation tools that help move projects from concept to bankable reality. The Department of Commerce and State are working together right now on a program called Technical Assistance for Bankable Infrastructure in Africa, which is supporting African governments to develop bankable projects that can attract U.S. participation and deliver local value. It’s a model designed to empower African partners rather than create dependency. Third, we proudly champion open, competitive, and transparent markets. Our work on commercial diplomacy, data governance, and investment partnerships with countries such as Kenya, Nigeria, Cote d’Ivoire reflect a commitment to fair regulatory environments that unlock innovation and protect sovereignty. When African nations choose U.S. partners, they gain collaborators who strengthen their capacity to negotiate effectively, diversify supply chains, and shape global standards. And finally, the United States uniquely integrates economic, security, and technological cooperation from supporting secure digital systems – ecosystems, excuse me – to reinforcing logistics, like corridors in the Lobito, helping build the enabling environment that makes long-term commercial success possible. We don’t just build projects; we build the conditions for sustainable growth. In short, our integrated approach to partnership based on mutual benefit, high standards, transparent governance, local value creation, and a long-term commitment is what distinguishes the United States in a crowded landscape of global actors. MODERATOR: Great, thank you for that. Our next question is also from Nigeria. It goes to Brigadier General Filcek, who asks about readiness. “The symposium is all about boosting our collective readiness. How does USAFRICOM objectively assess whether African partners are genuinely becoming more operationally self-sufficient instead of just leaning more on U.S. logistical support?” BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Thank you for that question. We are fostering lasting partnerships with significant progress acceleration through our A3I program. A3I is Assess, Advise, Advocate, and Integrate. This provides targeted and meaningful military engagement to identify and address their most urgent operational needs in order to expand their capacity to nurture independence. This approach will increase regional interoperability and partner ties to better facilitate commercial industry investments across Africa (inaudible). Ultimately, our joint (inaudible) litmus tests, where our partners can showcase rapid improvements and we can gauge how well USAFRICOM is transitioning to supporting and advising roles. MODERATOR: Okay, thank you for that. Thank you. Our third question goes back to DAS Mitchell, also from Nigeria, who asks: “With your extensive background in artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, how can African countries leverage AI to enhance logistics and supply chains while steering clear of over-reliance on foreign technologies and ensuring data sovereignty?” MR MITCHELL: A very good question, thank you. The opportunity is real and fast returning. AI can transform African logistics through route optimization, through predictive fleet maintenance, demand forecasting, faster customs and border processing, all critical for a continent whose competitiveness depends on the cost and reliability of moving goods, and for knitting together the AfCFTA single market. Sovereignty doesn’t mean building the whole stack. Complete technological self-containment is unrealistic for any country, because the AI stack is too complex. Real AI sovereignty means owning and using best-in-class technology for the benefit of your people and nation, strategic autonomy alongside rapid adoption – not isolation while you try and ultimately fail to build self-sufficiency. Keep your data yours. American companies can build large, independent AI infrastructure with secure and robust supply chains that minimize backdoor risk, plus cryptographically protect confidentiality, and world-leading security to keep sensitive logistics and trade data within your borders and under your control. Build on the infrastructure you own, adapted to your context. When American companies build it, it’s yours. Open-source models enable local training and fine tuning with linguistic and cultural adaptation, without embedded political orthodoxies. And logistics AI works to best build on local road networks, trade patterns, and local data sets and partners. And in doing so, choose your ecosystem carefully and choose American. The real choice is not which chip or cloud to buy, but which ecosystem powers your growth for the next generation. Not every ecosystem offers the same performance, security, transparency, IP protection, commercial choice, or respect for national sovereignty. The American ecosystem does, and we win on the merits in open competition. And finally, AI and the secure digital trade infrastructure go hand in hand. By establishing strong data governance norms, auditability, and interoperability standards, African governments can negotiate from a position of strength with the external vendors, ensuring that any AI used in ports and corridors’ custom systems comply with national rules and support their long-term industrial development. MODERATOR: Thank you. And DAS Mitchell, I understand that you need to depart for your next engagement right away in this busy symposium, so we want to thank you for joining us. We’ll continue the call with Brigadier General Filcek, but we want to thank you for joining us today. MR MITCHELL: Thank you. MODERATOR: Sure thing. Thank you. Okay, moving right along then, we have another question for Brigadier General Filcek, which is: “What does AFRICOM gain by replacing the West Africa Logistics Conference with this broader symposium now?” BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Thank you for that question. It’s kind of an intuitive one to ask since we’ve done the conferences separately in the past. But in response, the easy answer is that in modern defense, logistics and communications can no longer be considered discretely. They share too many convergence points. National – or I’m sorry, natural progression would have us harmonize them as an enterprise so that they can best support each other. Having the opportunity to talk with so many partner-nation senior logistics leaders here, I’ve learned firsthand some examples of crucial interdependencies, one of which is a reliable infrastructure and supply support that wholly enables leading-edge interoperable communications suites. Without the logistics, the suites simply will not perform, and without the suite, operations would not exist. So in that (inaudible) construct, the two are inseparable. If on the first day (inaudible) forces characterize logistics as the spine and communications as the nervous system. The two are inseparable, and I don’t see a point in the future at which we would ever separate them (inaudible). MODERATOR: Brigadier General Filcek, you cut out a little bit at the end. I believe that was – were you finished with your answer to that question? BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: It depends, sir, on where I cut out. MODERATOR: Oh, okay. BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Did you catch the part where I (inaudible) said that I’ve learned firsthand the (inaudible) — MODERATOR: Okay. Ladies and gentlemen, we – this is – we seem to have a small technical difficulty, but we are – we are switching microphones so that you all can hear more clearly Brigadier General Paul Filcek. So please just give us one second here. Thank you. BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Hey, thank you for that. Can you acknowledge that you can hear me? MODERATOR: Now we hear you loud and clear. Thank you. BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Beautiful. In the interest of clarity, I think I’m going to go through the entirety of the response. MODERATOR: Sure thing. Thank you. BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Okay. So in modern defense, logistics and communications can no longer be considered discretely, because they share too many convergence points and inseparable interdependencies. Natural progression would have us harmonize them as an enterprise so that they can best support each other. Having the opportunity to talk with so many partner-nation senior logistics leaders here, I’ve learned firsthand examples of crucial interdependencies, one of which is that reliable infrastructure and supply support wholly enables leading-edge interoperable communication suites, and you cannot have one without the other. Over. MODERATOR: Thank you for that. Great, thank you. Okay, another question on emerging technology, this one also from Nigeria. The question is: “Beyond drones, which emerging logistics technologies – like, for example, predictive maintenance, AI-assisted supply chains, autonomous transport, or additive manufacturing – do you think will have the most significant impact on African defense capabilities in the next decade?” BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Yeah, I particularly appreciated this question, and the answer is that nobody can tell because it’s moving so fast. But I have something set aside for this crowd. The African continent provides challenges truly unique among theaters. This complicates what can be done where to what economies of scale, what economies of scope, and to what effect. The most significant advances will come through modular expeditionary capabilities – those our partners can procure incrementally at the pace of their internal or external investments that provide rapid transportability and access over vast distances and challenging conditions. Investments in local supply chains, infrastructure, and secure trade corridors, for examples, will provide the most profound impact. And of course, all options can and should have modern aspects like predictive maintenance and targeted AI. Coincidentally, AFRICOM’s A3I program uses generative AI during the advise phase to supplement analysis and provide individual partner nations their own country logistics reports. Over. MODERATOR: Thank you for that. Thank you. And we have time for one last question that comes from the Ghana News Agency, which is that: “Ghana has long been regarded as a reliable U.S. security partner in West Africa. Are there any new initiatives or areas of cooperation with Ghana expected to emerge from the ALCS26, particularly in logistics, air mobility, or military training?” BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Thank you for that question. Yes, that’s the easy answer, is yes. Ghana is a robust partner to USAFRICOM and has already completed its initial A3I program survey and entered into the program in the advise and advocacy phase, and USAFRICOM has continual military-to-military engagements that yields significant value continuously. Over. MODERATOR: Okay. Great. I believe that is – that is all the time we have. I realize for those of you on the call, that we were not able to get to all of the questions, but we do appreciate those of you who posed questions and joined us today. I’d like to thank our guests today. Thank you, Deputy Assistant Secretary Mark Mitchell, and also thanks to Brigadier General Paul G. Filcek for taking time out of the Africa Logistics and Communications Symposium to brief us about it. A recording and a transcript of today’s briefing will be distributed to all registered journalists. If you have any questions about today’s briefing, you may also contact us at the Africa Regional Media Hub, our address is AFMedia@state.gov. If you publish any articles or broadcasts from today’s briefing please do share a link with us at that same email address. And I’d also like to invite you all, invite everyone, to follow us on X at our handle, @AfricaMediaHub. For our French speaking participants, please also join us at the handle @USAenFrancais. And thank you all. I wish you a very pleasant day, and thank you, and a great success for the rest of the symposium.

Our job is to experiment, adapt, test, learn, and move quickly to bring logistics and communications technologies and sustainment programs that actually work in African conditions. Logistics and communications, industry partnerships, regional cooperation and interoperability – these are not the exciting aspects of defense and security, but they are the elements that ultimately determine success or failure, victory or defeat. Our intent for this African Logistics and Communications Symposium is to strengthen our partnerships, share challenges that can generate shared solutions, and cultivate investments into capabilities that will keep our nation secure and our people protected. Thank you, and I welcome your questions. MODERATOR: Great, thank you. Thank you, Brigadier General Paul G. Filcek. We’ll now begin the question-and-answer portion of today’s briefing, but please be aware that it will not be possible to answer all of your questions in the short time that we have today. With that, our first question today will go to Fishe Media from Nigeria, who asked about competing global influence. And his question is – this is directed to DAS Mitchell – “African nations are engaging with the United States, China, the European Union, Türkiye, and Gulf States all at once. What unique value does the United States believe it brings to African partners that sets it apart from these other players?” MR MITCHELL: Thank you for the question. It’s true, African nations today have more options for global partners than ever, and that is a good thing. Here’s the value proposition that I think sets the United States apart. First, the U.S. approach is rooted in long-term enterprise-driven partnership, not one-off transactions. Our private sector invests for the long term, helping to build durable commercial ecosystems that strengthen the local institutions, they’re deep in the regulatory capacity, and that expand opportunities for African firms and workers. We see this in sectors like energy, digital infrastructure, critical minerals, and logistics, all areas where American companies deliver world-class technology, transparency, and high-standard operations that reinforce resilience and good governance. Second, the United States brings high-quality finance, trusted standards, and risk mitigation tools that help move projects from concept to bankable reality. The Department of Commerce and State are working together right now on a program called Technical Assistance for Bankable Infrastructure in Africa, which is supporting African governments to develop bankable projects that can attract U.S. participation and deliver local value. It’s a model designed to empower African partners rather than create dependency. Third, we proudly champion open, competitive, and transparent markets. Our work on commercial diplomacy, data governance, and investment partnerships with countries such as Kenya, Nigeria, Cote d’Ivoire reflect a commitment to fair regulatory environments that unlock innovation and protect sovereignty. When African nations choose U.S. partners, they gain collaborators who strengthen their capacity to negotiate effectively, diversify supply chains, and shape global standards. And finally, the United States uniquely integrates economic, security, and technological cooperation from supporting secure digital systems – ecosystems, excuse me – to reinforcing logistics, like corridors in the Lobito, helping build the enabling environment that makes long-term commercial success possible. We don’t just build projects; we build the conditions for sustainable growth. In short, our integrated approach to partnership based on mutual benefit, high standards, transparent governance, local value creation, and a long-term commitment is what distinguishes the United States in a crowded landscape of global actors. MODERATOR: Great, thank you for that. Our next question is also from Nigeria. It goes to Brigadier General Filcek, who asks about readiness. “The symposium is all about boosting our collective readiness. How does USAFRICOM objectively assess whether African partners are genuinely becoming more operationally self-sufficient instead of just leaning more on U.S. logistical support?” BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Thank you for that question. We are fostering lasting partnerships with significant progress acceleration through our A3I program. A3I is Assess, Advise, Advocate, and Integrate. This provides targeted and meaningful military engagement to identify and address their most urgent operational needs in order to expand their capacity to nurture independence. This approach will increase regional interoperability and partner ties to better facilitate commercial industry investments across Africa (inaudible). Ultimately, our joint (inaudible) litmus tests, where our partners can showcase rapid improvements and we can gauge how well USAFRICOM is transitioning to supporting and advising roles. MODERATOR: Okay, thank you for that. Thank you. Our third question goes back to DAS Mitchell, also from Nigeria, who asks: “With your extensive background in artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, how can African countries leverage AI to enhance logistics and supply chains while steering clear of over-reliance on foreign technologies and ensuring data sovereignty?” MR MITCHELL: A very good question, thank you. The opportunity is real and fast returning. AI can transform African logistics through route optimization, through predictive fleet maintenance, demand forecasting, faster customs and border processing, all critical for a continent whose competitiveness depends on the cost and reliability of moving goods, and for knitting together the AfCFTA single market. Sovereignty doesn’t mean building the whole stack. Complete technological self-containment is unrealistic for any country, because the AI stack is too complex. Real AI sovereignty means owning and using best-in-class technology for the benefit of your people and nation, strategic autonomy alongside rapid adoption – not isolation while you try and ultimately fail to build self-sufficiency. Keep your data yours. American companies can build large, independent AI infrastructure with secure and robust supply chains that minimize backdoor risk, plus cryptographically protect confidentiality, and world-leading security to keep sensitive logistics and trade data within your borders and under your control. Build on the infrastructure you own, adapted to your context. When American companies build it, it’s yours. Open-source models enable local training and fine tuning with linguistic and cultural adaptation, without embedded political orthodoxies. And logistics AI works to best build on local road networks, trade patterns, and local data sets and partners. And in doing so, choose your ecosystem carefully and choose American. The real choice is not which chip or cloud to buy, but which ecosystem powers your growth for the next generation. Not every ecosystem offers the same performance, security, transparency, IP protection, commercial choice, or respect for national sovereignty. The American ecosystem does, and we win on the merits in open competition. And finally, AI and the secure digital trade infrastructure go hand in hand. By establishing strong data governance norms, auditability, and interoperability standards, African governments can negotiate from a position of strength with the external vendors, ensuring that any AI used in ports and corridors’ custom systems comply with national rules and support their long-term industrial development. MODERATOR: Thank you. And DAS Mitchell, I understand that you need to depart for your next engagement right away in this busy symposium, so we want to thank you for joining us. We’ll continue the call with Brigadier General Filcek, but we want to thank you for joining us today. MR MITCHELL: Thank you. MODERATOR: Sure thing. Thank you. Okay, moving right along then, we have another question for Brigadier General Filcek, which is: “What does AFRICOM gain by replacing the West Africa Logistics Conference with this broader symposium now?” BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Thank you for that question. It’s kind of an intuitive one to ask since we’ve done the conferences separately in the past. But in response, the easy answer is that in modern defense, logistics and communications can no longer be considered discretely. They share too many convergence points. National – or I’m sorry, natural progression would have us harmonize them as an enterprise so that they can best support each other. Having the opportunity to talk with so many partner-nation senior logistics leaders here, I’ve learned firsthand some examples of crucial interdependencies, one of which is a reliable infrastructure and supply support that wholly enables leading-edge interoperable communications suites. Without the logistics, the suites simply will not perform, and without the suite, operations would not exist. So in that (inaudible) construct, the two are inseparable. If on the first day (inaudible) forces characterize logistics as the spine and communications as the nervous system. The two are inseparable, and I don’t see a point in the future at which we would ever separate them (inaudible). MODERATOR: Brigadier General Filcek, you cut out a little bit at the end. I believe that was – were you finished with your answer to that question? BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: It depends, sir, on where I cut out. MODERATOR: Oh, okay. BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Did you catch the part where I (inaudible) said that I’ve learned firsthand the (inaudible) — MODERATOR: Okay. Ladies and gentlemen, we – this is – we seem to have a small technical difficulty, but we are – we are switching microphones so that you all can hear more clearly Brigadier General Paul Filcek. So please just give us one second here. Thank you. BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Hey, thank you for that. Can you acknowledge that you can hear me? MODERATOR: Now we hear you loud and clear. Thank you. BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Beautiful. In the interest of clarity, I think I’m going to go through the entirety of the response. MODERATOR: Sure thing. Thank you. BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Okay. So in modern defense, logistics and communications can no longer be considered discretely, because they share too many convergence points and inseparable interdependencies. Natural progression would have us harmonize them as an enterprise so that they can best support each other. Having the opportunity to talk with so many partner-nation senior logistics leaders here, I’ve learned firsthand examples of crucial interdependencies, one of which is that reliable infrastructure and supply support wholly enables leading-edge interoperable communication suites, and you cannot have one without the other. Over. MODERATOR: Thank you for that. Great, thank you. Okay, another question on emerging technology, this one also from Nigeria. The question is: “Beyond drones, which emerging logistics technologies – like, for example, predictive maintenance, AI-assisted supply chains, autonomous transport, or additive manufacturing – do you think will have the most significant impact on African defense capabilities in the next decade?” BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Yeah, I particularly appreciated this question, and the answer is that nobody can tell because it’s moving so fast. But I have something set aside for this crowd. The African continent provides challenges truly unique among theaters. This complicates what can be done where to what economies of scale, what economies of scope, and to what effect. The most significant advances will come through modular expeditionary capabilities – those our partners can procure incrementally at the pace of their internal or external investments that provide rapid transportability and access over vast distances and challenging conditions. Investments in local supply chains, infrastructure, and secure trade corridors, for examples, will provide the most profound impact. And of course, all options can and should have modern aspects like predictive maintenance and targeted AI. Coincidentally, AFRICOM’s A3I program uses generative AI during the advise phase to supplement analysis and provide individual partner nations their own country logistics reports. Over. MODERATOR: Thank you for that. Thank you. And we have time for one last question that comes from the Ghana News Agency, which is that: “Ghana has long been regarded as a reliable U.S. security partner in West Africa. Are there any new initiatives or areas of cooperation with Ghana expected to emerge from the ALCS26, particularly in logistics, air mobility, or military training?” BRIGADIER GENERAL FILCEK: Thank you for that question. Yes, that’s the easy answer, is yes. Ghana is a robust partner to USAFRICOM and has already completed its initial A3I program survey and entered into the program in the advise and advocacy phase, and USAFRICOM has continual military-to-military engagements that yields significant value continuously. Over. MODERATOR: Okay. Great. I believe that is – that is all the time we have. I realize for those of you on the call, that we were not able to get to all of the questions, but we do appreciate those of you who posed questions and joined us today. I’d like to thank our guests today. Thank you, Deputy Assistant Secretary Mark Mitchell, and also thanks to Brigadier General Paul G. Filcek for taking time out of the Africa Logistics and Communications Symposium to brief us about it. A recording and a transcript of today’s briefing will be distributed to all registered journalists. If you have any questions about today’s briefing, you may also contact us at the Africa Regional Media Hub, our address is AFMedia@state.gov. If you publish any articles or broadcasts from today’s briefing please do share a link with us at that same email address. And I’d also like to invite you all, invite everyone, to follow us on X at our handle, @AfricaMediaHub. For our French speaking participants, please also join us at the handle @USAenFrancais. And thank you all. I wish you a very pleasant day, and thank you, and a great success for the rest of the symposium.

items.title: Xasan Sheekh oo kulan miro-dhal ah la yeeshay Museveni
items.description: Kampala (Caasimada Online) – Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Federaalka Soomaaliya, Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud ayaa galinkii dambe ee maanta safar shaqo ku gaaray magaalada Kampala ee caasimadda dalka Uganda, halkaas oo uu kulan miro-dhal ah kula yeeshay dhiggiisa Uganda, Yoweri Kaguta Museveni. Kulanka labada madaxweyne ayaa diiradda lagu saaray xoojinta xiriirka taariikhiga ah ee u dhexeeya Soomaaliya iyo Uganda iyo sidii loo sii ambaqaadi lahaa iskaashiga labada dal ee dhinacyada kala duwan. Labada hoggaamiye ayaa si gaar ah uga wada-hadlay iskaashiga dhinacyada amniga, la dagaallanka kooxaha argagixisada, horumarinta hay’adaha dowladda iyo xoojinta wada-shaqeynta gobolka si loo xaqiijiyo nabad iyo xasillooni waarta oo ka hanaqaadda Geeska Afrika. Uganda ayaa ka mid ah dalalka ciidamada ugu badan ku leh Soomaaliya, iyadoo door muuqda ka qaadatay howl-galladii Midowga Afrika ee lagu taageerayay dowladda federaalka, waxaana labada dhinac ay carrabka ku adkeeyeen muhiimadda sii wadista iskaashiga amniga. Sidoo kale, Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh iyo Madaxweyne Museveni ayaa is dhaafsaday aragtiyo ku saabsan shir-madaxeedka dalalka ciidamadoodu ka qeyb qaataan howl-galka Midowga Afrika ee Taageerada iyo Xasillinta Soomaaliya (AUSSOM), kaas oo berri ka furmaya magaalada Kampala. Shirkan ayaa la filayaa in diiradda lagu saaro xaaladda amniga Soomaaliya, taageerada howl-galka AUSSOM, iyo sidii loo dardargelin lahaa dadaallada lagu xoojinayo awoodda hay’adaha amniga iyo geeddi-socodka dowlad-dhiska dalka. Labada madaxweyne ayaa ugu dambeyn adkeeyay muhiimadda ay leedahay in beesha caalamku sii waddo taageerada ay siiso Soomaaliya, si loo xaqiijiyo amni, xasillooni siyaasadeed iyo horumar waara, iyagoo muujiyay in iskaashiga gobolka uu laf-dhabar u yahay guusha dadaalladaas. The post Xasan Sheekh oo kulan miro-dhal ah la yeeshay Museveni appeared first on Caasimada Online .

items.title: Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh oo hambalyeeyay shacabka Galmudug, kuna ammaanay doorashadii nabadda ku dhacday
items.description: Muqdisho – Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Federaalka Soomaaliya, Mudane Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud, ayaa hambalyo iyo bogaadin u diray shacabka Soomaaliyeed, gaar ahaan shacabka Galmudug, kadib markii si nabad ah ay uga qabsoontay doorashadii ka dhacday deegaannada Dowlad Goboleedka Galmudug. Madaxweynaha ayaa ku tilmaamay doorashadaasi guul taariikhi ah oo muujisay biseyl siyaasadeed iyo horumar dhinaca dimuqraadiyadda ah, isagoo sheegay in shacabka Galmudug ay muujiyeen masuuliyad, wadajir iyo kalsooni. Sidoo kale, Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh ayaa u mahadceliyay madaxda Galmudug, Guddiga Doorashooyinka, hay’adaha amniga, ururrada siyaasadda iyo dhammaan shacabka kaalintii ay ka qaateen qabsoomidda doorashada iyo sugidda amniga. Madaxweynaha ayaa xusay in odayaasha, hooyooyinka iyo dhallinyarada ay si sharaf iyo ilbaxnimo leh uga qayb qaateen doorashada, isla markaana qaar badan oo ka mid ah ay markii ugu horreysay codkooda ku dhiibteen doorasho toos ah. Wuxuu sheegay in tani ay caddeyn u tahay sida ay bulshada Soomaaliyeed uga go’an tahay xoojinta dimuqraadiyadda iyo in codka muwaadinku noqdo saldhigga hoggaanka dalka. Dhanka kale, Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh ayaa bogaadiyay ururrada siyaasadda ee ka qayb galay ololaha doorashada, isagoo sheegay inay muujiyeen tartan nabdoon oo ku dhisan is-ixtiraam, u hoggaansanaanta sharciga iyo ilaalinta midnimada bulshada. Ugu dambeyn, Madaxweynaha ayaa caddeeyay in Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya ay ka go’an tahay dib u soo celinta xuquuqda dastuuriga ah ee shacabka, gaar ahaan xaqa ay u leeyihiin inay si xor iyo xalaal ah u doortaan hoggaankooda, isagoo adkeeyay in codka shacabka uu yahay tiirka dowladnimada, dimuqraadiyadda iyo horumarka Soomaaliya.

items.title: Iiraan oo sheegtay inay diyaarado ka burburisay Mareykanka, kana dishay saraakiil
items.description: Tehran (Caasimada Online) – Ilaalada Kacaanka Islaamiga ah ee Iiraan (IRGC) ayaa sheegtay inay weerar gantaallo ah ku qaadday saldhigga cirka ee Al-Azraq ee dalka Urdun. Weerarkan ayaa lagu burburiyay saddex diyaaradood oo dagaal oo nooca F-35 ah oo Mareykanku leeyahay, halka saddex kale ay soo gaareen dhaawacyo culus, sida ay sheegeen ilaalada kacaanka Iiraan. War-saxaafadeed ay soo saartay waaxda xiriirka dadweynaha ee IRGC ayaa lagu sheegay in weerarka uu sidoo kale bartilmaameedsaday hangar lagu rakibo laguna dayactiro diyaaradaha dagaalka ee saldhigga Al-Azraq. Waxay intaas ku dareen in weerarkaasi ay ku dhinteen dhowr sarkaal oo Mareykan ah iyo shaqaale farsamo, inkastoo aysan sheegin tirada rasmiga ah ee khasaaraha. Ilaalada Kacaanka ayaa sheegtay in weerarkan uu jawaab u ahaa duqeymo ay sheegeen in ciidamada Mareykanku ka fuliyeen laba guri oo la degganaa oo ku yaalla Jasiiradda Qeshm ee Iiraan. Sida ay sheegeen, duqeymahaas waxaa ku dhintay saddex xubnood oo ka tirsanaa hal qoys, oo uu ku jiray hal cunug, halka laba carruur ah oo kale ay ku dhaawacmeen. Dhanka kale, dowladda Mareykanka weli kama aysan hadlin sheegashada Iiraan ee la xiriirta burburinta diyaaradaha F-35 ama khasaaraha la sheegay inuu soo gaaray ciidamadeeda. Sidoo kale, dowladda Urdun ayaan ilaa hadda soo saarin wax war rasmi ah oo xaqiijinaya ama beeninaya weerarka lagu sheegay inuu ka dhacay saldhigga Al-Azraq. Ilaa iyo hadda ma jiraan ilo madax-bannaan oo xaqiijiyay sheegashada IRGC. Sawirro dayax-gacmeed, muuqaallo ama caddeymo kale oo lagu xaqiijin karo burburka diyaaradaha ama khasaaraha saldhigga ayaan weli la soo bandhigin, taas oo adkeyneysa in si madax-bannaan loo xaqiijiyo wararka kasoo baxay Tehran. Saldhigga cirka ee Al-Azraq ayaa ka mid ah xarumaha militari ee muhiimka ah ee Urdun, waxaana marar kala duwan isticmaala ciidamada cirka ee Urdun iyo kuwa xulafada reer Galbeedka, oo uu ku jiro Mareykanka. Saldhiggan ayaa leh muhiimad istaraatiiji ah maadaama uu ku dhow yahay goobaha ay ka socdaan xiisadaha Bariga Dhexe. Sheegashadan cusub ayaa imaneysa xilli uu sii xoogeysanayo iska horimaadka u dhexeeya Mareykanka iyo Iiraan, iyadoo labada dhinac ay is dhaafsanayaan weerarro iyo eedeymo la xiriira hawlgallada militari ee gobolka.
